newsitem.title: CANADA: Plugged In: More stuffy ideas for Fido's news album.
newsitem.headline: Plugged In: More stuffy ideas for Fido's news album.

text.p: Why can't we stuff computers into newspapers rather than always trying to cram newspapers into computers?
That was the central question of last week's Plugged In column and it elicited some fun and ingenious e-mail responses.
The idea is that perhaps we need a whole new device to get our news as both newspapers and their electronic cousins are falling short of their marks.

Newsapers made from dead trees are getting a little tired when compared with the wired versions on the Internet. But when we try to fit newspapers onto video screens in the form of MSNBC or CNN's Internet site, sometimes the results are less than satisfying.
The news is interesting and stimulating with pictures, video and sounds, but does it really go well with your morning brew or with your favorite bubble bath?

So Plugged In offered up a portable device called a News Album: "Imagine a device like a photo album with a strong outer covering and thin but sturdy pages. The pages and the cover could be embedded with computer chips programmed to display numerous stories and headlines. Other chips would run videos or pictures in areas with built-in liquid display screens. Sound bites could be delivered via razor-thin speakers on the inside covers of the album.

The album could be plugged into a docking station each night where the pages would be refitted with a variety of news items, pictures and videos. The album could be thrown into a brief case and read on planes planes, trains, and in treehouses.
"I can't wait! I've been saying this for a long time," said one reader named Michael. "I want to leaf through pages and never have to mess with computer issues."

Some readers said they have either heard of the idea before or maintained it was something just around the corner. "The implementation of that idea is not particularly far off," said one reader from a "ThinLine" business unit.

One reader, Richard Owen, said such a device could be used by people with less than perfect eye sight where readers "could adjust the font size and brightness to compensate for our own aging, organic eyes."

Daniel Monaghan went to town with all the possibilities of a news album by allowing e-mail connections and even a video camera for instant conferencing. "And if people didn't want to carry their "slab" around they could rent one for a couple of bucks at the coffee shop, already pre-downloaded with info."

Some suggested that you really wouldn't need to turn the pages of the News Album because the device could simulate the action with a video screen. That is true but readers have become accustomed to having control over their books and newspapers and are attached to the look and feel of thumbing back and forth in books and newspapers.
As well, the concept must be kept simple so manufacturers would not be tempted to add "enhancements" that would never really work as promised.

Other connections to allow e-mail and other communications would be a selling point for the user and advertisers. Companies might love it if readers, taking a break from the up-to-date diet of death and destruction from around the world, took a few minutes to order flowers after scanning a video from XYZ Flower Co. on a News Album page.
Some readers also suggested an album format might work well for magazines, and books that could be updated with a few chapters each week.

Book albums (Bookums anyone?) and magazines (Magums?) could come with pictures, videos and graphics to enhance the reading experience. As well, how about an interview with the author that could be played before you tackle the tome? Or let's have an electronic dictionary to help you cope with a particularly pedantic scribbler.
An electronic index would be a godsend for a reader named Bob Goodfliesh. "That would also address one of my pet requests: the ability to search texts for some key item I want to revisit."
--For ideas and comments on the weekly Plugged In column send e-mail to russell.blinch(at)reuters.com
